newsitem.title: INDIA: Kashmir set for polls amid safety fears.
newsitem.headline: Kashmir set for polls amid safety fears.

text.p: Tens of thousands of Indian security officers fanned out across the Himalayan region of Kashmir on Friday ahead of local polls and amid concerns for the safety of candidates and voters.
Most businesses and shops were closed on Friday in Srinagar, the summer capital of Jammu and Kashmir state, at the start of a 48-hour protest strike called by separatists.
About 200,000 security officers were on duty for Saturday's first round of polling in the state, which has about eight million people.
Saturday's voting in the first local assembly elections since a separatist rebellion began six years ago were to be in 26 of 87 constituencies. Polls were due to open at 0130 GMT.
Other areas were to vote on September 16, 21 and 30 to let polling officers and security forces move between regions.

The election is viewed as a test of Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's strategy for restoring democratic rule to a region where more than 20,000 people have been killed in insurgency-related violence in six years.

Jammu and Kashmir is mostly Hindu India's only Moslem majority state. Militant groups here have been fighting either for independence or merger with neighbouring Pakistan, which rules one-third of the Kashmir region and claims the rest.
Most of these groups have threatened to disrupt the polling.
Police fired one tear gas shell to disperse about a dozen youths who shouted anti-election slogans in central Srinagar on Friday.
Most businesses and shops in the city were closed following a protest strike called by the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, which includes about 30 separatist groups.
Hurriyat leaders have toured the Kashmir Valley, a focus of the rebellion, urging voters to boycott the assembly polls.
Hurriyat chiefs said they had been held by security officials several times in the past two weeks, most recently on Thursday, and that they had been beaten.
They said Yasin Malik, head of the Jammu and Kashmir Liberation Front, had been taken to a Srinagar hospital after being beaten while in custody.
Mainstream parties have alleged that former militants now linked to the government have attacked their candidates during campaigning, which officially ended on Thursday.
Mufti Mohammad Sayed, an ex-Indian home minister and a Congress party candidate, said he was dissatisfied with security arrangements.
"No political party is satisfied with the arrangements," Sayed told Reuters in Jammu, the state's winter capital.

Former chief minister Farooq Abdullah, head of the National Conference party and tipped to become the next chief minister, renewed a threat to withdraw from the polls unless former militants contesting the elections were disarmed.
During the Indian general elections in May, human rights groups alleged widespread coercion in Jammu and Kashmir. Government officials denied the charges.
On Friday, London-based Amnesty International expressed concern at the lack of election observers and said that human rights abuses "could reach a new peak" during the election.

Amnesty said it had urged India to "take adequate measures to ensure that human rights defenders, including journalists, can carry out their activities without fear for their lives and safety, and to ensure that no one is compelled by violent means or the threat of violence to cast their votes."
India has let diplomats and journalists travel to Kashmir, which has been under direct rule from New Delhi since 1990, but it has barred groups of election observers from the state.
